state.misconception_label: Ignores negative sign when expanding bracket

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: John is expanding these three brackets: \( (x+5)(x-3)(x+6) \) He finds it helpful to split the first bracket and view the problem as follows: \( x(x-3)(x+6)+5(x-3)(x+6) \) He expands the brackets further. Before he simplifies, what are the terms than contain an \( \boldsymbol{x}^{2} \) ? I got \( \begin{array}{l}+6 x^{2} \\ +3 x^{2} \\ +5 x^{2}\end{array} \) because I forgot that two negatives multiply to a positive.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let me ask you this: what would happen if you tried your method on a simpler version of the problem with just two brackets instead of three?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, so if I try it with just two brackets, like \( (x+5)(x-3) \), I guess I would do \( x(x-3) + 5(x-3) \). But I’m still not sure how to keep track of the negative sign. Would I get a negative term when I multiply \( x \) with \( -3 \)?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let me ask you this: what do you notice about the sign of the term when you multiply \( x \) with \( -3 \) in the expression \( x(x-3) \)?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think when I multiply \( x \) with \( -3 \), I should get \( -3x \), right? So that means I have to remember that the negative sign is important when I'm expanding. But I'm still not sure how that affects the \( x^2 \) terms when I do it with three brackets. Can you help me see how to keep track of the signs better?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the sign-ignoring misconception by scaffolding down to two brackets and using focused questions that prompt reasoning about negative signs, leading the student to recognize that x × (-3) = -3x, though the student hasn't yet fully applied this insight back to the original three-bracket problem.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking, never directly provides answers, and strategically simplifies the problem to help the student discover their own misconceptions about sign tracking.
